primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'wise' primarily denotes the person who fears God and orders life according to His word — practical, moral-spiritual skill in godly living rather than mere intellect. The wise person hears and obeys God's instruction, and this wisdom is repeatedly said to begin with 'the fear of the LORD.' In the New Testament this is sharpened into hearing and doing the words of Christ, and into possessing the 'wisdom from above' that is given by God rather than the wisdom of the world.

alternatives.meaning: Christological/personified Wisdom: 'Wisdom' as a personified figure (Lady Wisdom) in Proverbs, read by much of the Christian tradition as a type or figure of Christ, who is 'the wisdom of God.'

Eschatological readiness: the 'wise' as those spiritually prepared and watchful for the Lord's return, in contrast to the foolish who are unprepared (wise vs. foolish virgins; the faithful and wise servant).
Negative/ironic sense: 'wise' as worldly or self-referential wisdom that God rejects — being 'wise in one's own eyes' or wise 'according to the flesh,' which Scripture treats as folly before God.

Wisdom as a charismatic gift or Spirit-endowment: being 'wise' as a special enablement given by the Holy Spirit for leadership, craftsmanship, or discernment (Bezalel, Joseph, Solomon, the gift of the 'word of wisdom').
The 'wise men' (Magi) of the nativity read symbolically as the Gentiles or the seeking soul drawn to worship Christ; a homiletical rather than lexical use of 'wise.'

notes: There is broad, recognizable consensus that biblical wisdom is fundamentally religious and practical — reverent obedience to God ('the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom') expressed in righteous conduct — rather than intellectual attainment. The main interpretive complexity is that 'wise' carries a deliberate double sense in Scripture: God-given wisdom (praised) versus worldly or self-styled wisdom (condemned), and readers must note which sense a passage intends. The Christological reading of personified Wisdom in Proverbs 8 is historically prominent (patristic and Reformation exegesis) though many modern scholars treat Lady Wisdom as a literary personification of God's attribute rather than a direct reference to Christ.
